title: Design and construction of sewers
summary: The self-cleansing velocity of 0.6 to 0.8 m/s and the maximum of 3 m/s are the two figures everything else hangs on — the first stops solids depositing, the second stops the invert abrading. The other high-value item is the partial-flow behaviour of a circular sewer: maximum discharge occurs at about 0.94 of full depth and maximum velocity at about 0.81, so a sewer running absolutely full is LESS efficient than one running nearly full. For Nepal, the separate system is the right choice because of monsoon intensity.

sections.heading: Systems of sewerage and quantity of flow
sections.body:
**Three systems**, and the choice is decided chiefly by rainfall:

| System | Carries | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Separate** | **Sewage and stormwater in SEPARATE sewers** | Treatment plant sees only sewage, so it is **small and not overwhelmed** by storms; no untreated overflow; stormwater can be discharged locally without treatment | **Two sets of sewers** — higher capital cost; the sanitary sewer is small and may need flushing |
| **Combined** | **Both together in one sewer** | **One set of sewers** — cheaper to build; the sewer is self-cleansing in storms | **Huge treatment plant** or **storm overflows discharging untreated sewage**; pumping costs rise |
| **Partially separate** | Sewage plus roof and yard drainage; road stormwater separate | Compromise; fewer connections | Some of both problems |

**The separate system is the right choice for Nepal**, and the reason is quantitative: monsoon rainfall intensity is high enough that a combined sewer would carry perhaps **fifty to a hundred times** the dry-weather flow in a storm. A treatment plant sized for that is absurd, so a combined system would necessarily have **storm overflows discharging raw sewage into rivers** during every significant rain — which is exactly the situation in many older Indian and European cities and is what modern practice avoids.

**Quantity of sanitary sewage:**

> **Average sewage flow ≈ 0.80 × water supply**

The **0.8 factor** allows for water that never reaches the sewer — irrigation of gardens, evaporation, drinking and cooking losses, and distribution losses that never entered a house at all.

**Additions and variations:**

| Item | Allowance |
|---|---|
| **Infiltration** (groundwater entering through joints and cracks) | 5 – 10% of the flow, or per length and diameter |
| Inflow (illegal storm connections, manhole covers) | Site-specific |
| **Peak factor for design** | **2 – 3** × average |
| **Minimum flow** | About **⅓ of the average** — used to check self-cleansing velocity |

**Both extremes must be checked**, and this is the design discipline of the subchapter:

> The sewer must have adequate **capacity at the PEAK flow**
> and adequate **VELOCITY at the MINIMUM flow**

A sewer designed only for the peak may run so shallow in the early morning that solids deposit and the invert silts up. That is the practical reason large sewers are difficult in small towns — and why a **separate** system's small sanitary sewers sometimes need periodic **flushing**.

**Quantity of stormwater** is computed by the **rational method**:

> **Q = C I A / 3.6**  (Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in km²)

with the **design storm duration taken as the time of concentration**, and a **return period** much shorter than for other structures:

| Drainage | Return period |
|---|---|
| **Residential storm drain** | **2 years** |
| Commercial and important areas | **5 years** |
| High-value or high-risk areas | 10 – 25 years |
| Major culvert or bridge | 50 – 100 years |

**Why so short?** Because the **consequence of exceedance is temporary surface flooding**, not structural failure or loss of life. Designing an urban drain for a 100-year storm would be enormously expensive to avoid an inconvenience that occurs briefly. The design accepts that the drain will surcharge occasionally, and the streets then act as the overflow route — which is why urban drainage design also considers the **surface flow path**.

**Urbanisation raises both the peak and the speed of runoff**, since paving increases C and reduces the time of concentration. A drain sized for the land use at the time of design is therefore inadequate within a decade in a growing town — which is why storm drainage must be designed for the **future** land use, and why **stormwater retention** and permeable surfaces are increasingly required.

sections.heading: Hydraulic design of sewers
sections.body:
**Sewers are designed as open channels**, not pressure pipes — they flow **partly full under gravity**, and the design uses **Manning's equation**:

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

with **n = 0.013** for a well-laid concrete or vitrified clay sewer (0.011 for smooth PVC, 0.015 for rough or old concrete).

**The two velocity limits — the foundation of the whole subchapter:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum (self-cleansing)** | **0.6 – 0.8 m/s** | Below it, **solids deposit** and the sewer silts up; organic deposits then decompose and generate H₂S |
| **Maximum (non-scouring)** | **3.0 m/s** | Above it, the suspended grit **abrades the invert**, destroying the pipe's smooth lining and eventually its structure |

**Self-cleansing velocity** is derived from the **Shields criterion** for the shear stress needed to move a particle of a given size and density:

> **V = (1/n) R^{1/6} √[(8 K/f)(G − 1) d]**

The practical outcome is that **larger sewers need a smaller gradient** to be self-cleansing, because their greater hydraulic radius gives more velocity for the same slope. That is why gradients flatten as sewers get bigger — a fact worth understanding rather than memorising the table.

**Minimum gradients** to achieve self-cleansing velocity:

| Diameter | Minimum gradient (approximate) |
|---|---|
| **150 mm** | **1 in 100** |
| 200 mm | 1 in 150 |
| 250 mm | 1 in 200 |
| **300 mm** | **1 in 300** |
| 450 mm | 1 in 500 |
| 600 mm | 1 in 700 |
| 900 mm | 1 in 1000 |

**Minimum diameter** for a public sewer is **150 mm** (200 mm in some standards) — not because a smaller pipe lacks capacity, but because it is liable to **blockage** by the objects that inevitably enter a sewer, and cannot be cleaned by rodding.

**Partial flow — the most valuable idea in the subchapter.** A circular sewer's discharge and velocity do **not** peak when it is full:

| Depth ratio d/D | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **0.81** | **MAXIMUM VELOCITY** |
| **0.94** | **MAXIMUM DISCHARGE** |
| 1.00 (full) | **Less** than the maximum of both |
| 0.50 | Velocity equals the full-flow velocity; discharge is half |

**Why.** As the water rises above about 0.8D, the **wetted perimeter increases faster than the area** — near the crown the added width of pipe wall contributes much more friction than the sliver of added area contributes flow. So the **hydraulic radius R = A/P falls**, and with it the velocity.

The consequence is practical: **a sewer running absolutely full is less efficient than one running nearly full**, and it also loses its ventilation. This is why sewers are conventionally designed to run at **not more than 0.7 to 0.8 of full depth** at the peak flow — leaving air space for **ventilation** and a margin for underestimated flow.

The **hydraulic elements (partial flow) diagram** plots v/V and q/Q against d/D and is used to find the depth and velocity at any flow — the standard design tool, and a graph a candidate should be able to describe.

**Shape of section:**

| Shape | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Circular** | **The standard** — best hydraulically for full flow, easiest to manufacture, structurally strong |
| **Egg-shaped (ovoid)** | **Combined** sewers with widely varying flow — the narrow invert maintains velocity at low flow |
| Horseshoe, semi-elliptical | Very large sewers, tunnels |
| Rectangular, trapezoidal | Large storm drains, open channels |
| U-shaped, parabolic | Storm drains |

**The egg-shaped section's rationale** is worth stating: in a combined sewer the dry-weather flow is a tiny fraction of the storm flow, so a circular section would run so shallow in dry weather that solids deposit. The narrow lower portion of an ovoid concentrates the small flow into a deeper, faster stream — self-cleansing at low flow while retaining capacity above. Its costs are difficult manufacture and structural weakness, which is why circular sections dominate the **separate** system where the flow range is smaller.

**Design procedure for a sanitary sewer**, in sequence:

1. Determine the **contributing population** and the **average sewage flow** (0.8 × water supply).
2. Apply the **peak factor** to get the design flow, and compute the **minimum flow** (about ⅓ average).
3. Assume a **diameter and gradient** (following the ground slope where possible, to minimise excavation).
4. Compute the **full-flow capacity and velocity** by Manning.
5. Using the **partial flow diagram**, find the **depth and velocity at the peak flow** — check d/D ≤ 0.8.
6. Find the **velocity at the minimum flow** — check it reaches **self-cleansing**.
7. Check the **maximum velocity** ≤ 3 m/s.
8. Adjust the diameter or gradient and repeat if any check fails.

Step 6 is the one most often skipped, and it is the check that prevents a silted sewer.

sections.heading: Sewer materials, appurtenances and construction
sections.body:
**Materials:**

| Material | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Vitrified clay (stoneware)** | **Excellent corrosion and abrasion resistance**, smooth | Brittle, small sizes, many joints |
| **Cement concrete (RCC / NP class)** | Strong, any size, cast in situ possible | **Attacked by acids and H₂S**; needs lining in aggressive conditions |
| **PVC / HDPE** | Corrosion-free, light, smooth, **flexible** | Deforms under load if not properly bedded; UV degradation |
| Cast iron | Strong, watertight | Corrodes; used where pressure or crossings demand |
| Steel | Pressure mains, outfalls | Corrosion |
| Brick | Large sewers, historic | Labour intensive; needs rendering |
| Asbestos cement | Historic | No longer used |

**Crown corrosion is the characteristic failure of a concrete sewer** and deserves explanation because it is examined:

1. Under **anaerobic** conditions in the sewage (which develop wherever the flow is slow or septic), sulphates are reduced to **H₂S**;
2. The H₂S is released into the **air space above the water**;
3. **Aerobic bacteria on the moist crown** oxidise it to **sulphuric acid**;
4. The acid attacks the cement, and the **crown of the sewer corrodes away** while the invert, always submerged, remains sound.

The controls follow from the mechanism: **maintain self-cleansing velocity** (so the sewage does not go septic), provide **ventilation** (so H₂S does not accumulate), and use **sulphate-resisting cement or a protective lining** in vulnerable sewers.

**Sewer appurtenances and their duties** — a reliable source of one-line questions:

| Appurtenance | Duty | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Manhole** | **Access** for inspection, cleaning and rodding | Every change of **direction, gradient or diameter**, at junctions, and on straight runs at intervals |
| **Drop manhole** | Where the incoming sewer is much **higher** than the outgoing — **dissipates energy** | At a steep fall |
| **Inspection chamber** | Smaller access point | House connections |
| **Lamp hole** | Historic; allowed a lamp to check alignment | Superseded by CCTV |
| **Inverted siphon** | Carries the sewer **under** an obstruction, flowing **full and under pressure** | Under a river, road or another pipe |
| **Catch basin / gully trap** | Intercepts **grit and debris** before entry | Street inlets |
| **Flushing tank** | Provides a **flush** to scour a sewer with insufficient flow | Dead-end and upper reaches |
| **Grease and oil trap** | Intercepts grease | Kitchens, garages, industries |
| **Ventilating column** | Releases **foul gases** | On long sewers, at intervals |
| **Storm overflow** | Discharges excess flow | Combined systems only |
| Regulator / flow divider | Controls flow split | — |

**Manhole spacing:**

| Sewer size | Spacing |
|---|---|
| Up to 300 mm | **30 – 45 m** |
| 300 – 600 mm | 45 – 75 m |
| Above 600 mm | 75 – 100 m (up to 150 m for man-entry sizes) |

The spacing is set by the **reach of cleaning equipment** — a rod or jetting hose must reach from one manhole to the next — rather than by any hydraulic requirement.

**The inverted siphon is worth understanding** because it is a genuine design problem. It flows **full and under pressure**, so it **cannot be scoured by gravity** and will silt up unless the velocity is maintained. The standard solution is **multiple parallel barrels** with inlets at different levels: the smallest barrel carries the dry-weather flow at self-cleansing velocity, and the others come into operation only as the flow rises. Each barrel is provided with a **penstock** so it can be isolated and cleaned.

**Construction of a sewer:**

1. **Setting out** the line and level, with **sight rails and boning rods** to control the invert level precisely — a sewer's gradient is often 1 in 500, so a few centimetres of error over a length destroys it.
2. **Excavation** of the trench, with **timbering or sheeting** where the depth or soil requires.
3. **Dewatering** if below the water table.
4. **Bedding** — granular or concrete, to distribute the load and support the pipe uniformly. This is critical for **flexible pipes (PVC, HDPE)**, which rely on the **side support of the surrounding soil** for their strength; a flexible pipe laid on poorly compacted bedding deflects and fails.
5. **Laying** from the **downstream end upward**, with the socket facing upstream.
6. **Jointing**, and **testing**.
7. **Backfilling** in compacted layers, taking care not to disturb the pipe.

**Testing:** the **water (hydrostatic) test** for watertightness at a specified head, the **air test** as a quicker alternative, the **smoke test** to locate defective joints and illegal connections, and the **ball or mandrel test** for alignment and deformation. Modern practice adds **CCTV inspection**, which is now the standard way of surveying an existing sewer.

**Rigid or flexible pipe** is a distinction worth knowing: a **rigid** pipe (concrete, clay) carries the load in the **pipe wall** and fails by cracking; a **flexible** pipe (PVC, HDPE) **deflects** and transfers load to the surrounding soil, so its performance depends entirely on the **quality of the sidefill compaction**. Specifying a flexible pipe and then backfilling carelessly is a common and expensive error.

**Safety in sewer work** must be stated because sewer entry kills people every year. Sewers contain **H₂S** (which is heavier than air, collects at the invert, and **deadens the sense of smell** so the warning disappears as the danger rises), **methane** (explosive), and **oxygen-deficient** atmospheres. A sewer or deep manhole is a **confined space**, and entry requires **gas testing before and during**, **forced ventilation**, a **harness and lifeline** with attendants above, and a **permit-to-work** system. The rule that matters most: **never enter on the assumption that it is safe because it looks or smells all right.**

formulas.label: Quantity of sanitary sewage
formulas.expression: average flow ≈ 0.80 × water supply ;   design peak factor 2–3 ;   minimum flow ≈ ⅓ average
formulas.note: Both extremes must be checked: capacity at peak, self-cleansing velocity at minimum.

formulas.label: Velocity limits
formulas.expression: self-cleansing minimum 0.6–0.8 m/s ;   non-scouring maximum 3.0 m/s
formulas.note: Below the minimum, solids deposit and go septic; above the maximum, grit abrades the invert.

formulas.label: Manning's equation for sewers
formulas.expression: V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2},  n = 0.013 for concrete or vitrified clay
formulas.note: Sewers are designed as OPEN channels flowing partly full, not as pressure pipes.

formulas.label: Partial flow in a circular sewer
formulas.expression: maximum VELOCITY at d/D = 0.81 ;   maximum DISCHARGE at d/D = 0.94
formulas.note: Both exceed the full-flow values, because near the crown the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area.

formulas.label: Design depth of flow
formulas.expression: Design for d/D ≤ 0.7 to 0.8 at the peak flow
formulas.note: Leaves air space for ventilation and a margin for underestimated flow.

formulas.label: Minimum gradients
formulas.note: Larger sewers need flatter gradients because their greater hydraulic radius gives more velocity.

formulas.label: Stormwater by the rational method
formulas.expression: Q = C I A/3.6, with the storm duration equal to the time of concentration
formulas.note: Return period only 2–5 years for urban drains, because exceedance means temporary flooding, not failure.

formulas.label: Manhole spacing
formulas.note: Set by the reach of cleaning equipment, not by hydraulics.
